passage: The substitute teacher had to leave the class alone for twenty minutes, and the room got loud. Amandeep sat very straight, finishing the map worksheet exactly as the instructions said. His group was making a poster on rivers, and Jatin, the group leader, drew the Ganga flowing into the Arabian Sea. Amandeep knew it was wrong. He had read it last night. He opened his mouth, then closed it. Everyone else was nodding. What if Jatin got annoyed? What if they called him a know-it-all? He coloured the river carefully the wrong way. At the end the teacher came back and said, "Who drew this? It goes to the Bay of Bengal." Amandeep stared at his crayon, cheeks burning.

qa.q: Where did Jatin draw the Ganga flowing into?
qa.a: Into the Arabian Sea.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep close his mouth instead of correcting Jatin?
qa.a: He was afraid Jatin would get annoyed or that the group would call him a know-it-all, so fear of disapproval kept him quiet.

qa.q: What could Amandeep try next time he knows something the group has wrong?
qa.a: He could say it gently, like 'I read it goes to the Bay of Bengal, shall we check?', which keeps the peace and still shares what he knows.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel if Amandeep had spoken up?
qa.a: Jatin might have felt a moment of surprise, but probably would have been glad to fix the poster before the teacher saw it.

grounding: A rule-following child keeps quiet about a mistake to avoid upsetting the group, burying what he knows.

passage: At home, Manoj talked in his Nani's Bhojpuri, full of jokes and funny words. At his new school in Delhi, he didn't say a single one. He copied how Siddharth and the other boys spoke, wore his socks pulled up exactly like them, and never forgot his tie. When the class teacher asked for ideas for the class trip, Manoj thought of the old stepwell near his Nani's house. He'd been there; it was amazing. But Siddharth said, "Let's just do the mall," and everyone agreed. Manoj stayed quiet. At home that night he told Nani about the stepwell in a rush of words. "Why didn't you say it in class?" she asked. Manoj shrugged. "Nobody else said anything different."

qa.q: What did Manoj think of for the class trip?
qa.a: The old stepwell near his Nani's house.

qa.q: Why does Manoj stay quiet about the stepwell?
qa.a: He wants to fit in and fears standing out, since nobody else said anything different from Siddharth.

qa.q: What small step could help Manoj share his own ideas at school?
qa.a: He could tell the teacher his idea privately or bring a photo of the stepwell, so it feels less risky than speaking up in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Nani see Manoj's quietness at school?
qa.a: Nani knows the chatty, funny boy at home, so she may be puzzled and a little sad that he hides that side in class.

grounding: A child copies classmates' dress and speech and holds back his own idea, fitting in at the cost of his own opinion.

passage: "How was the class vote, Sunaina?" Vikas asked, stirring the dal. "Fine, Papa. We're doing a skit on road safety." "I thought you wanted to do the one about the lake birds." Sunaina picked at the tablecloth. "Everyone else wanted road safety." "Did you say what you wanted?" "No. Ma'am likes it when we don't argue. And Pooja would think I'm showing off." Vikas sat down across from her. "Being polite is good. But your idea counts too." "What if they don't like it?" "Then they don't. But they'll know you had one." Sunaina was quiet. "Maybe I can ask Ma'am if the birds can be a poster instead." Vikas smiled. "That's a start."

qa.a: She decides to ask Ma'am if the lake birds can be a poster, a polite way to share her own idea without upsetting anyone.

passage:
I'm Sarita, I'm eleven, and I used to be the best-behaved girl in Class 6. I never forgot my ID card. I never ran in the corridor. I tied my hair in two plaits exactly like Himani and her friends, because they said one plait looked "weird."
In art, Miss told us to paint any sky. Everyone did orange sunsets. I wanted a purple sky with green clouds. I painted an orange sunset.
When the girls laughed at a new girl's accent, I didn't laugh, but I didn't say anything either. I was scared they'd stop sitting with me.
Then one day Himani asked me, "Sarita, what do you actually like?" And I couldn't answer. My mouth just opened. I went home and felt strange all evening, like I'd lost something without noticing.

qa.q: What did Sarita want to paint?
qa.a: A purple sky with green clouds.

qa.q: Why couldn't Sarita answer when Himani asked what she actually liked?
qa.a: She had followed the rules and the group for so long, fearing disapproval, that she had buried her own opinions and no longer knew them.

qa.q: At which moment could Sarita have made a different choice, and what might it have given her?
qa.a: In art class, she could have painted the purple sky; showing one small preference would have kept her own taste alive.

qa.q: How might the new girl have seen Sarita's silence when others laughed?
qa.a: The new girl might have thought Sarita agreed with the others, not knowing she was simply scared to speak.

grounding: It shows a child who follows every rule and copies the group's style to avoid disapproval, keeping the peace but burying her own opinions.

passage:
Class 5 note, Monday. Vidya Rao, class teacher.
Pranav follows every rule, perfectly. He raises his hand even to ask if he may sharpen a pencil. His uniform is always exact. When the class is noisy, he looks at me anxiously, as if he is the one in trouble.
Today we debated whether homework should be banned. Pranav agreed with whoever spoke last. When I asked for his own view, he said, "Whatever everyone thinks, ma'am."
But after class he waited until the room was empty and whispered, "Actually, I think homework helps, but I didn't want the others to be angry." He looked relieved and scared at the same time.
His politeness makes the class calmer. I worry he is hiding himself to keep the peace.
Next: I will set up a private opinion box so Pranav, and others like him, can share views without fear.

qa.q: What did Pranav whisper after class?
qa.a: Actually, I think homework helps, but I didn't want the others to be angry.

qa.q: Why did Pranav look relieved and scared at the same time?
qa.a: He was relieved to finally say what he thought, but scared that sharing an opinion might bring disapproval.

qa.q: Why is Vidya Rao's opinion box a good next step for Pranav?
qa.a: It gives him a safe way to share his real views without fearing others' anger, so his own voice can grow.

qa.q: How might Pranav's classmates see him?
qa.a: They probably see him as the polite, rule-following boy who never argues, not knowing he has opinions he keeps hidden.

grounding: It shows a child who follows every rule and agrees with the group to avoid disapproval, keeping harmony but burying his own opinion.
